subject_line: Goethe, Evie and Shai in Everything the Light Touches
email_body:
Dear Janice,

In Everything the Light Touches, Goethe travels through Italy as Johann Philipp Möller, Evie sets out from Cambridge to find the sacred forests of the Lower Himalayas, and Shai goes home to Shillong with no return date. You have called the tussle between fixity and fluidity the core of the book. I would like to ask how that idea shaped the structure itself: how did you decide where one traveller's story should give way to the next?

subject_line: Water on rock and the Tethys Sea
email_body:
Dear Anannya,

Your poem "Imprints of the Tethys Sea" in Usawa Literary Review stayed with me. It treats the vanished sea as something rock still remembers: water marks that carry a memory nobody now alive was there to have. You also make photographs, and a camera keeps traces in its own way. I would like to ask whether the poems and the pictures start from the same kind of looking, and whether that has changed since Between Sure Places.

subject_line: From Time Is a Fire to Gandhi Colony
email_body:
Dear Vikram,

I read on your site that an extract from your novel-in-progress, Gandhi Colony, was named co-winner of The Letter Review Prize for Books. Time Is a Fire opens in Seattle in 1997 and looks back to the violence of 1984 in Delhi, so I am curious whether Gandhi Colony comes back to the city from a closer distance, and how far teaching creative writing at Shiv Nadar has changed the way you draft a long book.

subject_line: Harish, Lahore and Yashpal's feminism in Dada Comrade
email_body:
Dear Simona,

In your introduction to Dada Comrade, the first English translation of Yashpal's 1941 novel, you write that Yashpal's feminism is not the same as yours, but that this does not stop you from recognising it as a feminism. That is a generous way to read an older writer. I would like to ask how that distance showed in the translating itself: were there scenes with Harish in pre-Independence Lahore where you had to choose between Yashpal's idiom and a contemporary reader's ear?

subject_line: Aunt Okane's art collection in Speed of Lightness
email_body:
Dear Barrie,

In Speed of Lightness, Aozora Fujiwara is a Kyoto University student sunk in mah-jong debt when his Aunt Okane, whose name means money, dies and leaves him and his sister Mai a collection of priceless art. A name like that is almost a joke the book plays on its own plot. I would like to ask how a thriller grew out of that set-up, and whether writing short fiction for The Angel Tiger and Other Stories changed how you paced a longer book.

Dear Samuel,

everything.is works with the textual and linguistic layers of the internet, and Ajar Press has now brought it out with a Vietnamese translation by Quyên Nguyễn-Hoàng. I came to it through "Forked Tongues", your Diacritics conversation with her and Nazry Bahrawi. Poems so bound up with the language of the internet seem very hard to carry into another language, so I would like to ask what the translation showed you about your own lines, and which poem you most expected to resist her.

قرأت أن روايتك «اختبال» الصادرة عام 2019 رُشّحت للجائزة العالمية للرواية العربية، وأنك في الوقت نفسه أستاذة للأدب العربي والمقارن في الجامعة الأمريكية في الشارقة ويدور جزء كبير من بحثك حول تأليف المرأة والتبادل الثقافي. يهمّني أن أسألك: هل تكتبين الرواية بعين الباحثة التي تدرس أصوات الكاتبات، أم أن الرواية مساحة تتحررين فيها من تلك العين تمامًا؟

subject_line: Tituba, Owen Hart and MOVE in Spectral Evidence
email_body:
Dear Gregory,

Spectral Evidence sets Tituba, the only Black woman accused of witchcraft at Salem, beside predictive policing, the wrestler Owen Hart and MOVE. It is an unlikely company, and the book makes the links between them feel inevitable. I would like to ask how that range took shape, and whether teaching and running the Literature and Creative Writing program at NYU Abu Dhabi, so far from those American histories, has changed how you look at them now.

subject_line: Tatreez, jasmine and entari in Life in a Country Album
email_body:
Dear Nathalie,

Life in a Country Album moves through four regions and gathers things that carry belonging in cloth and scent: tatreez from Bethlehem, the jasmine of Damascus, the Turkish entari worn at weddings. The book keeps asking who gets to decide who belongs. Since then you have been teaching in Abu Dhabi, another city of many arrivals. I would like to ask whether living there has added a new album, and what objects or languages would belong in it.

subject_line: The hunters, the herders and the hunted in Nairobi Noir
email_body:
Dear Peter,

In your introduction to Nairobi Noir you present the anthology as an excavation, a way to rediscover a segregated city, a concrete jungle of "the hunters and the herders and the hunted." Each of the fourteen stories is tied to a distinct part of Nairobi. I would like to ask how you chose which neighbourhoods had to be in the book, and whether editing it changed how you approach your own fiction after Dance of the Jakaranda.

book_title: For What Are Butterflies Without Their Wings
subject_line: The brother lost to the lake in your title story
email_body:
Dear Troy,

The title story of For What Are Butterflies Without Their Wings follows a sister who relives twenty years of rivalry after her brother disappears in a lake. It first won the fiction prize at the inaugural Nyanza Literary Festival in 2016, and six years later it gave its name to your Masobe Books collection. As someone who grew up in Kisumu, how much of the lake in that story is Lake Victoria, and did it change between prize and book?
